questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A black body is at temperature of 5780 K. The energy of radiation emitted by the body at wavelength 300 nm is $U_1$, at wavelength 500 nm is $U_2$ and that at 900 nm is $U_3$ respectively. Wien's constant $b = 2.89 \times 10^6\ \text{nmK}$. This shows that
questions.solution:
Using Wien's displacement law, $\lambda_m T = b$.

Substituting the given values:

$\lambda_m = \dfrac{2.89 \times 10^6}{5780} = 500 \text{ nm}$

The maximum energy of radiation is emitted at $\lambda_m = 500 \text{ nm}$.

Since $U_2$ corresponds to the energy at $500 \text{ nm}$, it is the maximum energy.

Therefore, $U_2 \gt U_1$ and $U_2 \gt U_3$.

This gives $U_1 \lt U_2 \gt U_3$.

Answer: $U_1 \lt U_2 \gt U_3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sphere having temperature 600 K is losing heat due to radiation. At this temperature its rate of cooling is $R$. The rate of cooling of this sphere at 400 K is $\dfrac{x}{243}$. The value of $x$ is (Temperature of surrounding is 300 K)
questions.solution:
The rate of cooling of a body is given by Stefan-Boltzmann law:

$R = \dfrac{dT}{dt} = \dfrac{e \sigma A}{ms} (T^4 - T_0^4)$

This implies $R \propto (T^4 - T_0^4)$.

For the first case, $T_1 = 600$ K and $T_0 = 300$ K:

$R_1 = k (600^4 - 300^4) = R$

For the second case, $T_2 = 400$ K and $T_0 = 300$ K:

$R_2 = k (400^4 - 300^4) = \dfrac{x}{243}$

Taking the ratio of $R_2$ to $R_1$:

$\dfrac{R_2}{R_1} = \dfrac{400^4 - 300^4}{600^4 - 300^4}$

$\dfrac{R_2}{R} = \dfrac{4^4 - 3^4}{6^4 - 3^4}$

$\dfrac{R_2}{R} = \dfrac{256 - 81}{1296 - 81}$

$\dfrac{R_2}{R} = \dfrac{175}{1215}$

Dividing the numerator and denominator by $5$:

$\dfrac{R_2}{R} = \dfrac{35}{243}$

$R_2 = \dfrac{35R}{243}$

Comparing this with the given rate of cooling $\dfrac{x}{243}$, we get:

$x = 35R$

Answer: $35R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A piece of metal of 850 K is dropped into 1 kg of water at 300 K. If equilibrium temperature of water is 350 K then the heat capacity of the metal expressed in $\dfrac{J}{K}$ is $\left(\text{Sp. heat of water} = 1\ \dfrac{\text{cal}}{\text{g}^\circ\text{C}}\right)$
questions.solution:
According to the principle of calorimetry, heat lost by the metal is equal to the heat gained by the water.

Heat gained by water is $Q = m_w s_w \Delta T_w$

Given mass of water $m_w = 1\text{ kg} = 1000\text{ g}$

Specific heat of water $s_w = 1\text{ cal/g}^\circ\text{C} = 4.2\text{ J/g}^\circ\text{C}$

Change in temperature of water $\Delta T_w = 350 - 300 = 50\text{ K}$

$Q = 1000 \times 4.2 \times 50 = 210000\text{ J}$

Heat lost by the metal is $Q = C \Delta T_m$

Change in temperature of the metal $\Delta T_m = 850 - 350 = 500\text{ K}$

Equating the heat lost to the heat gained:

$C \times 500 = 210000$

$C = \dfrac{210000}{500} = 420\text{ J/K}$

Answer: $420$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two stars A and B radiate maximum energy at wavelength $3.9 \times 10^{-7}$ m and $5.2 \times 10^{-7}$ m respectively. The ratio of the temperature of star A to that of star B will be
questions.solution:
Using Wien's displacement law, $\lambda_{m} T = b$ (constant).

Therefore, $\lambda_{A} T_{A} = \lambda_{B} T_{B}$

$\dfrac{T_{A}}{T_{B}} = \dfrac{\lambda_{B}}{\lambda_{A}}$

Substituting the given values:

$\dfrac{T_{A}}{T_{B}} = \dfrac{5.2 \times 10^{-7}}{3.9 \times 10^{-7}}$

$\dfrac{T_{A}}{T_{B}} = \dfrac{52}{39} = \dfrac{4}{3}$

The ratio of the temperature of star A to that of star B is $4 : 3$.

Answer: $4 : 3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two rods of same length, radius and material transfer a given amount of heat in 't' second when they are joined as shown in fig (1). But when they are joined as shown in fig (2) then they will transfer same heat in same condition in time
questions.solution:
Let the thermal resistance of each rod be $R$.

In figure (1), the two rods are connected in parallel. The equivalent thermal resistance is:
$R_p = \dfrac{R \times R}{R + R} = \dfrac{R}{2}$

The amount of heat transferred in time $t$ is:
$Q = \dfrac{\Delta T}{R_p} t = \dfrac{2 \Delta T}{R} t$

In figure (2), the two rods are connected in series. The equivalent thermal resistance is:
$R_s = R + R = 2R$

Let the time taken to transfer the same amount of heat $Q$ under the same temperature difference $\Delta T$ be $t'$. Then:
$Q = \dfrac{\Delta T}{R_s} t' = \dfrac{\Delta T}{2R} t'$

Equating the two expressions for $Q$:
$\dfrac{2 \Delta T}{R} t = \dfrac{\Delta T}{2R} t'$

$2t = \dfrac{t'}{2}$

$t' = 4t$

Answer: $4t$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A sphere is at temperature $600$ K. In an external environment of $200$ K, its cooling rate is R. When the temperature of the sphere falls to $400$ K then cooling rate R' will become
questions.solution:
According to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, the rate of cooling of a body is given by $R = \dfrac{dT}{dt} = \dfrac{e \sigma A}{ms}(T^4 - T_0^4)$.

For the first case, $T = 600$ K and $T_0 = 200$ K.

$R \propto (600^4 - 200^4)$

$R \propto 200^4(3^4 - 1^4) = 200^4(81 - 1) = 80 \times 200^4$

For the second case, $T = 400$ K and $T_0 = 200$ K.

$R' \propto (400^4 - 200^4)$

$R' \propto 200^4(2^4 - 1^4) = 200^4(16 - 1) = 15 \times 200^4$

Taking the ratio of the two rates:

$\dfrac{R'}{R} = \dfrac{15 \times 200^4}{80 \times 200^4} = \dfrac{15}{80} = \dfrac{3}{16}$

$R' = \dfrac{3}{16}R$

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{16}R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
$15$ g of ice at $0^\circ\text{C}$ is added to a vessel containing water at $40^\circ\text{C}$. The mass of water and water equivalent of the vessel is $60$ g. Assuming that negligible heat is taken from the surroundings, the final temperature of the mixture will be
[ $L_{\text{ice}} = 80\,\text{cal/g}$ , $S_{\text{water}} = 1\,\text{cal/g}$ ]
questions.solution:
Let the final temperature of the mixture be $T^\circ\text{C}$.

According to the principle of calorimetry, heat lost by the water and vessel equals the heat gained by the ice.

Heat lost by water and vessel = $m_{\text{water}} S_{\text{water}} (40 - T)$

Heat gained by ice = $m_{\text{ice}} L_{\text{ice}} + m_{\text{ice}} S_{\text{water}} (T - 0)$

Equating the two:

$60 \times 1 \times (40 - T) = 15 \times 80 + 15 \times 1 \times T$

$2400 - 60T = 1200 + 15T$

$75T = 1200$

$T = \dfrac{1200}{75} = 16^\circ\text{C}$

Answer: $16^\circ\text{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Out of the following, which statement is NOT true about black body radiation ?
options: Intensity is more for shorter wavelengths ($\lambda$).
Intensity is same for all wavelengths ($\lambda$).
Intensity is less for longer wavelengths ($\lambda$).
A black body emits all wavelengths ($\lambda$).
questions.solution:
A black body emits radiation of all wavelengths, forming a continuous spectrum.

According to Planck's law of black body radiation, the intensity of emitted radiation is not uniform across all wavelengths. The intensity increases with an increase in wavelength, reaches a maximum value at a specific wavelength (which depends on the temperature of the body), and then decreases for longer wavelengths.

Therefore, the statement that the intensity is the same for all wavelengths is incorrect.

Answer: Intensity is same for all wavelengths ($\lambda$).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the two temperatures on Fahrenheit scale differ by $54^\circ\text{F}$, then the difference in temperature on the Celsius scale is
questions.solution:
The relation between the Fahrenheit and Celsius temperature scales is given by:

$F = \dfrac{9}{5}C + 32$

Taking the difference for two temperatures, we get:

$\Delta F = \dfrac{9}{5}\Delta C$

Given that the difference on the Fahrenheit scale is $\Delta F = 54^{\circ}\text{F}$, substituting this value yields:

$54 = \dfrac{9}{5}\Delta C$

$\Delta C = 54 \times \dfrac{5}{9}$

$\Delta C = 30^{\circ}\text{C}$

The difference in temperature on the Celsius scale is $30^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Answer: $30^\circ\text{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A black body is at temperature $827^\circ\text{C}$. The rate at which it emits energy is proportional to
questions.solution:
According to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, the rate at which a black body emits energy is directly proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature.

$E \propto T^4$

The given temperature is $t = 827^\circ\text{C}$.

Converting this to absolute temperature in Kelvin:

$T = 827 + 273 = 1100 \text{ K}$

Therefore, the rate of energy emission is proportional to $(1100)^4$.

Answer: $(1100)^4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When $170$ J of energy is incident on a surface of a body, $17$ J of energy is reflected by it. If the coefficient of absorption is $0.7$, then the amount of energy transmitted will be
questions.solution:
Coefficient of reflection, $r = \dfrac{Q_r}{Q} = \dfrac{17}{170} = 0.1$

Coefficient of transmission, $t = 1 - (a + r) = 1 - (0.7 + 0.1) = 0.2$

Transmitted energy, $Q_t = t Q = 0.2 \times 170 = 34$ J

Answer: $34.0$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body cools from a temperature $3\theta$ to $2\theta$ in 10 minute. The room temperature is $\theta$. The temperature of the body at the end of the next 10 minute is '$x$'. Assuming that Newton's law of cooling is applicable, the value of '$x$' will be
questions.solution:
According to Newton's law of cooling, the temperature $T$ of a body at time $t$ is given by:

$T - T_0 = (T_i - T_0)e^{-kt}$

where $T_0$ is the surrounding temperature and $T_i$ is the initial temperature.

For the first 10 minutes, $T_i = 3\theta$, $T = 2\theta$, and $T_0 = \theta$:

$2\theta - \theta = (3\theta - \theta)e^{-10k}$

$\theta = 2\theta e^{-10k}$

$e^{-10k} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

For the next 10 minutes, the new initial temperature is $T_i = 2\theta$ and the final temperature is $x$:

$x - \theta = (2\theta - \theta)e^{-10k}$

$x - \theta = \theta \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$

$x = \theta + \dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2}\theta$

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{2}\theta$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A black body radiates maximum energy at wavelength '$\lambda$' at temperature $T_1$ and its emissive power is E. When the temperature of the body is changed to $T_2$, it radiates maximum energy at wavelength $\dfrac{2\lambda}{3}$, then the emissive power will become
questions.solution:
According to Wien's displacement law, $\lambda_{max} T = \text{constant}$.

$\lambda T_1 = \dfrac{2\lambda}{3} T_2$

$T_2 = \dfrac{3}{2} T_1$

According to Stefan-Boltzmann law, the emissive power $E$ is proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature, $E \propto T^4$.

$\dfrac{E_2}{E_1} = \left(\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^4$

$\dfrac{E_2}{E} = \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^4 = \dfrac{81}{16}$

$E_2 = \dfrac{81}{16} E$

Answer: $\dfrac{81}{16}\,E$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ratio of thermal conductivity of two rods of different materials is $4:3$. The two rods have same area of cross-section and same thermal resistance. The lengths of rods are in the ratio
questions.solution:
Thermal resistance is given by $R = \dfrac{L}{KA}$.

Given that the thermal resistances are equal ($R_1 = R_2$) and the areas of cross-section are equal ($A_1 = A_2$), we have:

$\dfrac{L_1}{K_1 A} = \dfrac{L_2}{K_2 A}$

$\dfrac{L_1}{L_2} = \dfrac{K_1}{K_2}$

Given the ratio of thermal conductivities $K_1 : K_2 = 4 : 3$, we get:

$\dfrac{L_1}{L_2} = \dfrac{4}{3}$

The lengths of the rods are in the ratio $4 : 3$.

Answer: $4 : 3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two spherical black bodies of radii $R_1$ and $R_2$ having surface temperature $T_1$ and $T_2$ respectively, radiate the same power. The ratio of $R_1$ to $R_2$ will be
questions.solution:
According to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, the power radiated by a spherical black body is given by $P = \sigma A T^4 = \sigma (4 \pi R^2) T^4$.

Given that both black bodies radiate the same power, $P_1 = P_2$.

$\sigma (4 \pi R_1^2) T_1^4 = \sigma (4 \pi R_2^2) T_2^4$

$R_1^2 T_1^4 = R_2^2 T_2^4$

$\dfrac{R_1^2}{R_2^2} = \dfrac{T_2^4}{T_1^4}$

$\dfrac{R_1}{R_2} = \left(\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^2$

Answer: $\left(\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a composite slab there are two materials having coefficients of thermal conductivity K and 2K, thickness x and 4x repectively. The temperature of the two outer surfaces of a composite slab are $T_2$ and $T_1(T_2 \gt  T_1)$. $T_2$ is on side K and $T_1$ is on side 2K. The rate of heat transfer through the slab in a steady state is $\left[\dfrac{A(T_2 - T_1)K}{x}\right] \cdot f$, where f is equal to
questions.solution:
The thermal resistance of a slab is given by $R = \dfrac{L}{KA}$, where $L$ is the thickness, $K$ is the thermal conductivity, and $A$ is the area of cross-section.

For the first material, the thermal resistance is $R_1 = \dfrac{x}{KA}$.

For the second material, the thermal resistance is $R_2 = \dfrac{4x}{2KA} = \dfrac{2x}{KA}$.

Since the two materials form a composite slab in series, the equivalent thermal resistance is:

$R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 = \dfrac{x}{KA} + \dfrac{2x}{KA} = \dfrac{3x}{KA}$

The rate of heat transfer through the slab in a steady state is given by:

$H = \dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{\dfrac{3x}{KA}} = \dfrac{KA(T_2 - T_1)}{3x}$

This can be rewritten as:

$H = \left[\dfrac{A(T_2 - T_1)K}{x}\right] \cdot \dfrac{1}{3}$

Comparing this with the given expression $H = \left[\dfrac{A(T_2 - T_1)K}{x}\right] \cdot f$, we get:

$f = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A black body emits radiation of maximum intensity of wavelength '$\lambda$' at temperature 'T' K. Its corresponding wavelength at temperature $(2.5T)$ K will be
questions.solution:
According to Wien's displacement law, the product of the wavelength corresponding to maximum intensity of emission and the absolute temperature of the black body is a constant.

$\lambda_{m} T = \text{constant}$

$\lambda_{1} T_{1} = \lambda_{2} T_{2}$

Given $\lambda_{1} = \lambda$, $T_{1} = T$, and $T_{2} = 2.5 T = \dfrac{5}{2} T$.

$\lambda \times T = \lambda_{2} \times \left(\dfrac{5}{2} T\right)$

$\lambda_{2} = \dfrac{2\lambda}{5}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider two rods 1 and 2 of same length. They have different specific heats $(C_1, C_2)$, thermal conductivities $(K_1, K_2)$ and area of cross-section $(A_1, A_2)$ respectively. Both the rods have temperatures $(T_1, T_2)$ at their ends. If their rate of loss of heat due to conduction is equal, then
questions.solution:
The rate of heat flow (or rate of loss of heat due to conduction) through a rod is given by Fourier's law of heat conduction:

$\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \dfrac{KA(T_1 - T_2)}{L}$

For the first rod, the rate of heat flow is:

$\left(\dfrac{dQ}{dt}\right)_1 = \dfrac{K_1 A_1 (T_1 - T_2)}{L}$

For the second rod, the rate of heat flow is:

$\left(\dfrac{dQ}{dt}\right)_2 = \dfrac{K_2 A_2 (T_1 - T_2)}{L}$

It is given that the rate of loss of heat due to conduction is equal for both rods. Equating the two rates:

$\dfrac{K_1 A_1 (T_1 - T_2)}{L} = \dfrac{K_2 A_2 (T_1 - T_2)}{L}$

Since the length $L$ and the temperature difference $(T_1 - T_2)$ are the same for both rods, they cancel out from both sides:

$K_1 A_1 = K_2 A_2$

Specific heat is not involved in the steady-state rate of heat conduction.

Answer: $A_1 K_1 = A_2 K_2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: '$x$' joule of heat is incident on a body. Out of it, the total heat reflected and transmitted by it is '$y$' joule. The absorption coefficient of the body is
questions.solution:
Total heat incident on the body is $Q = x$.

Total heat reflected and transmitted by the body is $Q_r + Q_t = y$.

From the conservation of energy, the total heat absorbed by the body is $Q_a = Q - (Q_r + Q_t) = x - y$.

The absorption coefficient is defined as the ratio of the heat absorbed to the total heat incident on the body.

$a = \dfrac{Q_a}{Q} = \dfrac{x - y}{x}$

Answer: $\dfrac{x-y}{x}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an external environment of temperature ($T$) kelvin, a sphere at temperature ($3T$) kelvin has cooling rate $R_1$. When the temperature of that sphere falls to ($2T$) kelvin, the cooling rate $R_2$ of the sphere will become
questions.solution:
According to Stefan-Boltzmann law, the rate of cooling of a body is given by $R = \dfrac{dT}{dt} = \dfrac{\sigma e A}{ms} (T_{body}^4 - T_{surr}^4)$.

Let $k = \dfrac{\sigma e A}{ms}$.

For the first case, the temperature of the sphere is $3T$ and the surroundings is $T$.

$R_1 = k((3T)^4 - T^4) = k(81T^4 - T^4) = 80kT^4$

For the second case, the temperature of the sphere falls to $2T$.

$R_2 = k((2T)^4 - T^4) = k(16T^4 - T^4) = 15kT^4$

Taking the ratio of $R_2$ to $R_1$:

$\dfrac{R_2}{R_1} = \dfrac{15kT^4}{80kT^4} = \dfrac{15}{80} = \dfrac{3}{16}$

$R_2 = \dfrac{3}{16}R_1$

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{16}R_1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bowl filled with very hot water cools from $98^\circ\text{C}$ to $86^\circ\text{C}$ in 2 minutes when the room temperature is $22^\circ\text{C}$. How long it will take to cool from $75^\circ\text{C}$ to $69^\circ\text{C}$ ?
questions.solution:
Using Newton's law of cooling:

$\dfrac{T_1 - T_2}{t} = K \left( \dfrac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_0 \right)$

For the first case:

$\dfrac{98 - 86}{2} = K \left( \dfrac{98 + 86}{2} - 22 \right)$

$6 = K (92 - 22)$

$6 = 70K \Rightarrow K = \dfrac{3}{35}$

For the second case:

$\dfrac{75 - 69}{t} = K \left( \dfrac{75 + 69}{2} - 22 \right)$

$\dfrac{6}{t} = K (72 - 22)$

$\dfrac{6}{t} = 50K$

Substituting the value of $K$:

$\dfrac{6}{t} = 50 \times \dfrac{3}{35}$

$\dfrac{6}{t} = \dfrac{30}{7}$

$t = \dfrac{42}{30} = 1.4 \text{ minutes}$

Answer: $1.4$ minute

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A black rectangular surface of area 'A' emits energy 'E' per second at $27^\circ$C. If length and breadth is reduced to half of its initial value and temperature is raised to $327^\circ$C then energy emitted per second becomes
questions.solution:
Initial temperature $T_1 = 27^{\circ}\text{C} = 300\text{ K}$

Initial area $A_1 = A$

Energy emitted per second $E = \sigma A T_1^4 = \sigma A (300)^4$

When length and breadth are reduced to half, the new area $A_2 = \dfrac{L}{2} \times \dfrac{B}{2} = \dfrac{A}{4}$

New temperature $T_2 = 327^{\circ}\text{C} = 600\text{ K}$

New energy emitted per second $E' = \sigma A_2 T_2^4$

$E' = \sigma \left(\dfrac{A}{4}\right) (600)^4$

$E' = \sigma \left(\dfrac{A}{4}\right) (2 \times 300)^4$

$E' = \sigma \left(\dfrac{A}{4}\right) \times 16 \times (300)^4$

$E' = 4 \sigma A (300)^4 = 4E$

Answer: $4E$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The energy spectrum of a black body exhibits a maximum around a wavelength '$\lambda$'. The temperature of the black body is now changed such that the energy is maximum around a wavelength $2\lambda/3$. The power radiated by the black body will now increase by a factor
questions.solution:
According to Wien's displacement law:

$\lambda_{m} T = b \Rightarrow T \propto \dfrac{1}{\lambda_{m}}$

Given $\lambda_{1} = \lambda$ and $\lambda_{2} = \dfrac{2\lambda}{3}$.

$\dfrac{T_{2}}{T_{1}} = \dfrac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{2}} = \dfrac{\lambda}{\dfrac{2\lambda}{3}} = \dfrac{3}{2}$

According to Stefan-Boltzmann law, the power radiated by a black body is given by:

$P = \sigma A T^{4} \Rightarrow P \propto T^{4}$

The ratio of final power to initial power is:

$\dfrac{P_{2}}{P_{1}} = \left(\dfrac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\right)^{4} = \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^{4} = \dfrac{81}{16}$

The power radiated increases by a factor of $\dfrac{81}{16}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{81}{16}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Rate of flow of heat through a cylindrical rod is '$H_1$'. The temperature at the ends of the rod are $T_1$ and $T_2$. If all the dimensions of the rod become double and the temperature difference remains the same and if the rate of flow of heat becomes '$H_2$' then $H_2 =$
questions.solution:
The rate of flow of heat through a rod is given by $H = \dfrac{KA(T_1 - T_2)}{L}$

For a cylindrical rod of radius $r$ and length $L$, the area of cross-section is $A = \pi r^2$.

Initial rate of heat flow is $H_1 = \dfrac{K \pi r^2 (T_1 - T_2)}{L}$

When all dimensions are doubled, the new radius is $r' = 2r$ and the new length is $L' = 2L$.

The new rate of heat flow is $H_2 = \dfrac{K \pi (2r)^2 (T_1 - T_2)}{2L}$

$H_2 = \dfrac{4 K \pi r^2 (T_1 - T_2)}{2L}$

$H_2 = 2 \left( \dfrac{K \pi r^2 (T_1 - T_2)}{L} \right)$

$H_2 = 2H_1$

Answer: $2\text{H}_1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The energy spectrum of a black body exhibits a maximum around a wavelength $\lambda$. The temperature of a black body is now changed such that the energy is maximum at wavelength $2\lambda/3$. The power radiated by the black body will now increase by a factor of
questions.solution:
Using Wien's displacement law, $\lambda_{m} T = b$

$\lambda_{1} T_{1} = \lambda_{2} T_{2}$

$\lambda T_{1} = \left(\dfrac{2\lambda}{3}\right) T_{2}$

$T_{2} = \dfrac{3}{2} T_{1}$

According to Stefan-Boltzmann law, the power radiated by a black body is $P = \sigma A T^{4}$

$P \propto T^{4}$

$\dfrac{P_{2}}{P_{1}} = \left(\dfrac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\right)^{4}$

$\dfrac{P_{2}}{P_{1}} = \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^{4} = \dfrac{81}{16}$

Answer: $\dfrac{81}{16}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A black rectangular surface of area A emits energy E per second at $127^\circ$C. If length and breadth is reduced to half of initial value and temperature is raised to $527^\circ$C then energy emitted becomes
questions.solution:
Using Stefan-Boltzmann law, the energy emitted per second by a black body is given by $E = \sigma A T^4$.

Initial temperature $T_1 = 127^\circ\text{C} = 400\text{ K}$
Initial area $A_1 = A$
Initial energy emitted $E_1 = \sigma A (400)^4 = E$

Final temperature $T_2 = 527^\circ\text{C} = 800\text{ K}$
Since length and breadth are reduced to half, the new area $A_2 = \dfrac{L}{2} \times \dfrac{B}{2} = \dfrac{A}{4}$

Final energy emitted $E_2 = \sigma A_2 T_2^4$

$E_2 = \sigma \left(\dfrac{A}{4}\right) (800)^4$

$E_2 = \dfrac{1}{4} \times 16 \times \sigma A (400)^4$

$E_2 = 4 \sigma A (400)^4 = 4E$

Answer: $4E$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ratio of the thermal conductivity of two rods of different materials is 6:5. The two rods of same area of cross section and same thermal resistance will have the length in the ratio
questions.solution:
Thermal resistance of a rod is given by $R = \dfrac{L}{KA}$

Given that both rods have the same thermal resistance ($R_1 = R_2$) and the same area of cross-section ($A_1 = A_2 = A$), we can write:

$\dfrac{L_1}{K_1 A} = \dfrac{L_2}{K_2 A}$

$\dfrac{L_1}{L_2} = \dfrac{K_1}{K_2}$

The ratio of thermal conductivities is given as $\dfrac{K_1}{K_2} = \dfrac{6}{5}$

Therefore, $\dfrac{L_1}{L_2} = \dfrac{6}{5}$

The lengths of the rods are in the ratio $6 : 5$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: About black body radiation, which one of the following is a WRONG statement?
options: For all wavelengths, power radiated is same
For shorter wavelengths, radiated power is more
for longer wavelengths, radiated power is less
All wavelengths are emitted by the black body
questions.solution:
According to the spectral distribution of black body radiation (Planck's law), a black body emits radiation of all possible wavelengths, but the energy is not uniformly distributed among them.

The spectral emissive power ($E_{\lambda}$) first increases with an increase in wavelength, reaches a maximum value at a specific wavelength ($\lambda_{m}$), and then decreases for longer wavelengths.

Therefore, the statement "For all wavelengths, power radiated is same" is completely incorrect.

Answer: For all wavelengths, power radiated is same

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A black disc has a radius 'R' and wavelength corresponding to the maximum intensity is '$\lambda$'. The emissive power (E) for the different radii and maximum wavelengths is directly proportional to
questions.solution:
The total emissive power of a black body is given by the Stefan-Boltzmann law:

$E = A \sigma T^4$

For a disc of radius $R$, the surface area $A \propto R^2$. Therefore, the emissive power is proportional to:

$E \propto R^2 T^4$

According to Wien's displacement law, the wavelength corresponding to maximum intensity $\lambda$ is related to the absolute temperature $T$ as:

$\lambda T = b$

$T \propto \lambda^{-1}$

Substituting this into the proportionality for $E$, we get:

$E \propto R^2 (\lambda^{-1})^4$

$E \propto R^2 \lambda^{-4}$

Answer: $R^2, \lambda^{-4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ordinary body cools from $4\theta$ to $3\theta$ in 't' minutes. The temperature of the body after next 't' minutes is (Assume Newton's law of cooling and room temperature as $\theta$)
questions.solution:
According to Newton's law of cooling, the temperature $T$ at time $t$ is given by:

$T - T_s = (T_i - T_s)e^{-kt}$

where $T_s$ is the surrounding temperature and $T_i$ is the initial temperature.

For the first $t$ minutes, $T_i = 4\theta$, $T = 3\theta$, and $T_s = \theta$:

$3\theta - \theta = (4\theta - \theta)e^{-kt}$

$2\theta = 3\theta e^{-kt} \Rightarrow e^{-kt} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

For the next $t$ minutes, the initial temperature is $3\theta$. Let the final temperature be $T'$:

$T' - \theta = (3\theta - \theta)e^{-kt}$

$T' - \theta = 2\theta \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = \dfrac{4\theta}{3}$

$T' = \theta + \dfrac{4\theta}{3} = \dfrac{7\theta}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{7\theta}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The coefficient of thermal conductivity of a metal rod depends on its
questions.solution:
The coefficient of thermal conductivity is an intrinsic property of a material. It depends only on the nature of the material and its temperature, and is independent of the dimensions of the rod such as length, area of cross-section, or mass.

Answer: material of the rod

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What will be the ratio of rate of radiation of metal sphere at two different temperatures $T_1 = 527^\circ$C and $T_2 = 127^\circ$C
questions.solution:
The temperatures in Kelvin are given by:

$T_1 = 527 + 273 = 800 \text{ K}$

$T_2 = 127 + 273 = 400 \text{ K}$

According to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, the rate of radiation $E$ is proportional to the fourth power of the absolute temperature $T$:

$E \propto T^4$

Taking the ratio of the rates of radiation at the two temperatures:

$\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \left(\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^4$

$\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \left(\dfrac{800}{400}\right)^4$

$\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = 2^4 = 16$

The ratio is $16:1$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A black rectangular surface of area A emits energy E per unit time at $27^\circ$ C. If length and breadth is reduced to $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{th}$ of initial value and temperature is raised to $327^\circ$ C, then energy emitted per unit time becomes
questions.solution:
According to Stefan-Boltzmann law, the energy emitted per unit time by a black body is given by $E = \sigma A T^4$.

Initial temperature $T_1 = 27^{\circ}\text{C} = 300\text{ K}$ and initial area $A_1 = A$.

Initial energy emitted per unit time is $E_1 = E = \sigma A (300)^4$.

Final temperature $T_2 = 327^{\circ}\text{C} = 600\text{ K}$.

Since length and breadth are reduced to $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of their initial values, the new area is $A_2 = \dfrac{L}{4} \times \dfrac{B}{4} = \dfrac{A}{16}$.

Final energy emitted per unit time is $E_2 = \sigma A_2 T_2^4$.

Taking the ratio of $E_2$ to $E_1$:

$\dfrac{E_2}{E_1} = \dfrac{A_2}{A_1} \left(\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^4$

$\dfrac{E_2}{E} = \dfrac{1}{16} \left(\dfrac{600}{300}\right)^4$

$\dfrac{E_2}{E} = \dfrac{1}{16} \times 2^4 = 1$

$E_2 = E$

Answer: $E$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Rate of radiation by a black body is 'R' at temperature 'T'. Another body has same area but emissivity is 0.2 and temperature 3T. Its rate of radiation is
questions.solution:
Rate of radiation for a black body is given by Stefan-Boltzmann law:

$R = \sigma A T^4$

For the second body, the rate of radiation is:

$R' = e \sigma A (T')^4$

Given $e = 0.2$ and $T' = 3T$, substituting these values:

$R' = 0.2 \times \sigma A (3T)^4$

$R' = 0.2 \times 81 \times \sigma A T^4$

$R' = 16.2 R$

Answer: $16.2R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A celsius and a Fahrenheit thermometer are dipped in boiling water. The temperature of water is lowered until the Farenheit thermometer shows $140^\circ$. What is the fall in temperature on the Celsius thermometer?
questions.solution:
The initial temperature of boiling water is $100^\circ$ C, which corresponds to $212^\circ$ F.

The final temperature is given as $140^\circ$ F.

The relationship between the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales is given by:

$\dfrac{C}{5} = \dfrac{F - 32}{9}$

Substituting $F = 140$:

$\dfrac{C}{5} = \dfrac{140 - 32}{9} = \dfrac{108}{9} = 12$

$C = 60^\circ$ C

The fall in temperature on the Celsius thermometer is the difference between the initial and final temperatures:

$\Delta C = 100^\circ \text{ C} - 60^\circ \text{ C} = 40^\circ \text{ C}$

Answer: $40^\circ$ C

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body cools in $7$ minutes from $60^\circ$C to $40^\circ$C. What time (in minutes) does it take to cool from $40^\circ$C to $28^\circ$C, if its surrounding temperature is $10^\circ$C ? (Newton's law of cooling holds good)
questions.solution:
Using Newton's law of cooling:

$\ln\left(\dfrac{T_1 - T_0}{T_2 - T_0}\right) = kt$

For the first interval, the body cools from $60^\circ$C to $40^\circ$C in $7$ minutes with surrounding temperature $T_0 = 10^\circ$C:

$\ln\left(\dfrac{60 - 10}{40 - 10}\right) = k(7)$

$\ln\left(\dfrac{50}{30}\right) = 7k$

$\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right) = 7k$

For the second interval, the body cools from $40^\circ$C to $28^\circ$C in time $t$:

$\ln\left(\dfrac{40 - 10}{28 - 10}\right) = kt$

$\ln\left(\dfrac{30}{18}\right) = kt$

$\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right) = kt$

Comparing the two equations, we get:

$kt = 7k \Rightarrow t = 7$ minutes.

Answer: $7$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The energy spectrum of a black body exhibits a maximum of wavelength $\lambda_0$. The temperature of the black body is now changed such that the energy is maximum at wavelength $\dfrac{3\lambda_0}{2}$. The ratio of power radiated by the black body will be
questions.solution:
Using Wien's displacement law, $\lambda_{m} T = \text{constant}$

$\lambda_1 T_1 = \lambda_2 T_2$

$\lambda_0 T_1 = \dfrac{3\lambda_0}{2} T_2$

$\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

According to Stefan-Boltzmann law, the power radiated by a black body is $P \propto T^4$

$\dfrac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^4$

$\dfrac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^4 = \dfrac{16}{81}$

Answer: $\dfrac{16}{81}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire of length $L$ and diameter $d$ is used in a bulb. The temperature of wire is $T$ and power radiated by the wire is $P$. Its emissivity is ($\sigma$ = Stefan's constant) (Assume that emissivity of wire material is same at all wavelength)
questions.solution:
According to Stefan-Boltzmann law, the power radiated by a body is given by $P = e \sigma A T^4$.

For a cylindrical wire of length $L$ and diameter $d$, the radiating surface area is $A = \pi d L$.

Substituting the area into the power equation gives $P = e \sigma (\pi d L) T^4$.

Rearranging for emissivity $e$, we get $e = \dfrac{P}{\sigma T^4 \pi d L}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{P}{\sigma T^4 \pi d L}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three identical heat conducting rods are connected in series as shown in the figure. The rods on the side have thermal conductivity $2K$ while that in the middle has thermal conductivity $K$. The left end of the combination is maintained at temperature $3T$ and the right end at $T$. The rods are thermally insulated from outside. In steady state, temperature at the left junction is $T_1$ and that at the right junctions is $T_2$. The ratio $T_1/T_2$ is
questions.solution:
Let the length of each rod be $L$ and the area of cross-section be $A$.

In steady state, the rate of heat flow is the same through all three rods:

$\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \dfrac{2KA(3T - T_1)}{L} = \dfrac{KA(T_1 - T_2)}{L} = \dfrac{2KA(T_2 - T)}{L}$

Cancelling $\dfrac{KA}{L}$ from all terms, we get:

$2(3T - T_1) = T_1 - T_2 = 2(T_2 - T)$

From the first and third parts of the equality:

$2(3T - T_1) = 2(T_2 - T)$

$3T - T_1 = T_2 - T$

$T_1 + T_2 = 4T \quad \dots (1)$

From the second and third parts of the equality:

$T_1 - T_2 = 2(T_2 - T)$

$T_1 - 3T_2 = -2T \quad \dots (2)$

Subtracting equation (2) from equation (1):

$(T_1 + T_2) - (T_1 - 3T_2) = 4T - (-2T)$

$4T_2 = 6T \Rightarrow T_2 = \dfrac{3T}{2}$

Substituting $T_2$ in equation (1):

$T_1 + \dfrac{3T}{2} = 4T \Rightarrow T_1 = \dfrac{5T}{2}$

The required ratio is:

$\dfrac{T_1}{T_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{5T}{2}}{\dfrac{3T}{2}} = \dfrac{5}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{5}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A black body has maximum wavelength ' $\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}$ ' at temperature 2000 K . Its maximum wavelength at 3000 K will be
questions.solution:
Wien's displacement law states that $\lambda_m T = b$, where $b$ is the Wien displacement constant, $\lambda_m$ is the peak wavelength, and $T$ is the absolute temperature. Consequently, $\lambda_m \propto \frac{1}{T}$.

For temperatures $T_1 = 2000$ K and $T_2 = 3000$ K, the corresponding peak wavelengths $\lambda_{m1}$ and $\lambda_{m2}$ satisfy $\lambda_{m1} T_1 = \lambda_{m2} T_2$.

Substituting the given $\lambda_{m1} = \lambda_m$ yields $\lambda_m \cdot 2000 = \lambda_{m2} \cdot 3000$, from which $\lambda_{m2} = \lambda_m \cdot \frac{2000}{3000} = \frac{2}{3} \lambda_m$.

The maximum wavelength at $3000$ K is $\frac{2}{3} \lambda_m$, corresponding to option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The outer surface of star in the form of a sphere radiates heat as a black body at temperature ' $T$ '. The total radiant energy per unit area, normal to the direction of incidence, received at a distance ' R ' from the centre of a star of radius ' r ' is ( $\mathrm{R}\gt \mathrm{r}$ ) ( $\sigma=$ Stefan's constant)
questions.solution:
The radiant energy per unit area received normal to incidence at distance $R$ from a star of radius $r$ radiating as a black body at temperature $T$ is determined through the Stefan-Boltzmann law and spherical radiation geometry.

The star's total radiative power is $P = \sigma (4\pi r^2) T^4$.

At distance $R$, this power distributes uniformly over the spherical surface area $4\pi R^2$, yielding the intensity $I = \frac{P}{4\pi R^2}$.

Substituting gives $I = \frac{\sigma (4\pi r^2) T^4}{4\pi R^2} = \frac{\sigma r^2 T^4}{R^2}$.

Final Answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The length of steel rod is 5 cm longer than the copper rod at all temperatures. The length of the steel and copper rod is respectively (Coefficient of linear expansion for steel and copper is respectively $1.1 \times 10^{-5} /{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $1.7 \times 10^{-5} /{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ )
questions.solution:
The constant length difference condition $L_s(T) - L_c(T) = 5\text{cm}$ must hold for all temperatures. Applying thermal expansion formulas $L(T) = L_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$ yields:

$(L_s - L_c) + (L_s\alpha_s - L_c\alpha_c)\Delta T = 5$

For temperature independence, both $L_s - L_c = 5$ and $L_s\alpha_s = L_c\alpha_c$ must be satisfied.

Substituting $L_s = L_c + 5$ into the second equation:

$(L_c + 5)\alpha_s = L_c\alpha_c$

$L_c = \frac{5\alpha_s}{\alpha_c - \alpha_s} = \frac{5 \times 1.1 \times 10^{-5}}{(1.7 - 1.1) \times 10^{-5}} = \frac{5.5}{0.6} \approx 9.17\text{cm}$

Thus $L_s = L_c + 5 \approx 14.17\text{cm}$.

These values correspond to nearly 14 cm and 9 cm, matching option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A liquid having coefficient of cubical expansion ' $\gamma$ ' is kept in a copper vessel having coefficient of linear expansion $\frac{\gamma}{3}$. If heat is supplied to the vessel, the original level of the liquid in the vessel will
questions.solution:
The coefficient of cubical expansion of the liquid is $\gamma_L = \gamma$, while the vessel's coefficient of linear expansion is $\alpha_V = \frac{\gamma}{3}$.
The cubical expansion coefficient for the vessel becomes $\gamma_V = 3\alpha_V = 3\left(\frac{\gamma}{3}\right) = \gamma$.

Given equal initial volumes $V_0$ and temperature change $\Delta T$,
the liquid expands by $\Delta V_L = V_0 \gamma \Delta T$ and the vessel's internal volume by $\Delta V_V = V_0 \gamma \Delta T$,
resulting in zero apparent volume change: $\Delta V_\text{app} = V_0(\gamma - \gamma)\Delta T = 0$.

The liquid level remains constant: $\boxed{C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two spherical black bodies have radii ' $r_1$ ' and ' $r_2$ '. Their surface temperatures are ' $\mathrm{T}_1$ ' and ' $\mathrm{T}_2$ '. If they radiate same power, then $\frac{\mathrm{r}_2}{\mathrm{r}_1}$ is
questions.solution:
The power radiated by a spherical black body follows the Stefan-Boltzmann law: $P = e \sigma A T^4$. Since emissivity $e = 1$ for a black body and $A = 4\pi r^2$, the power becomes $P = \sigma (4\pi r^2) T^4$.

Given two spherical black bodies with radii $r_1$, $r_2$ and temperatures $T_1$, $T_2$ radiating equal power, equate their expressions:

$\sigma (4\pi r_1^2) T_1^4 = \sigma (4\pi r_2^2) T_2^4$

Canceling the common factors $\sigma$ and $4\pi$ yields:

$r_1^2 T_1^4 = r_2^2 T_2^4$

Rearranging for the radius ratio:

$\frac{r_2^2}{r_1^2} = \frac{T_1^4}{T_2^4}$

Taking square roots of both sides gives the final relationship:

$\frac{r_2}{r_1} = \left(\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^2$

This corresponds to option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A calorimeter contains 10 g of water at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The temperature fall to $15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in 10 min . When calorimeter contains 20 g of water at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, it takes 15 min . for the temperature to become $15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The water equivalent at the calorimeter is
questions.solution:
Heat loss from a calorimeter occurs at a constant rate for a given temperature difference. The heat lost during cooling is $Q = (m_w + m_c) c_w \Delta T$, where $m_w$ is the water mass, $m_c$ is the calorimeter's water equivalent, and $\Delta T = 5^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in both cases.

For the first experiment with $m_w = 10\ \mathrm{g}$ and $t = 10\ \mathrm{min}$, the rate is $R = \frac{(10 + m_c) c_w \cdot 5}{10}$.

For the second with $m_w = 20\ \mathrm{g}$ and $t = 15\ \mathrm{min}$, $R = \frac{(20 + m_c) c_w \cdot 5}{15}$.

Equating rates gives $\frac{10 + m_c}{10} = \frac{20 + m_c}{15}$.

Solving, $15(10 + m_c) = 10(20 + m_c)$,
$150 + 15m_c = 200 + 10m_c$,
$5m_c = 50$,
$m_c = 10\ \mathrm{g}$.

The water equivalent is $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A black sphere has radius R whose rate of radiation is E at temperature T. If radius is made R/2 and temperature 3T, the rate of radiation will be
questions.solution:
Stefan-Boltzmann's Law gives the radiated power as $P = \sigma A T^4$, where $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $A$ is surface area, and $T$ is absolute temperature.

For a sphere with radius $R$, the area is $A = 4\pi R^2$, yielding $P = \sigma (4\pi R^2) T^4$.

Given initial radiation rate $E = \sigma (4\pi R^2) T^4$.

With radius halved to $R/2$ and temperature tripled to $3T$, the new radiation becomes:
$E' = \sigma \left[4\pi (R/2)^2\right] (3T)^4 = \sigma (4\pi R^2/4) (81T^4) = 81\sigma \pi R^2 T^4$.

From the initial condition, $\sigma \pi R^2 T^4 = E/4$, so $E' = 81(E/4) = \frac{81E}{4}$.

The new radiation rate is $\frac{81E}{4}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two black spheres P & Q have radii in the ratio $4: 3$. The wavelength of maximum intensity of radiation are in the ratio $4: 5$ respectively. The ratio of radiated power by P to Q is
questions.solution:
Wien's Displacement Law relates temperature and peak wavelength as $\lambda_{max} T = b$, so $T \propto 1/\lambda_{max}$. Given $\lambda_{max,P}/\lambda_{max,Q} = 4/5$, we find $T_P/T_Q = \lambda_{max,Q}/\lambda_{max,P} = 5/4$.

The Stefan-Boltzmann Law gives radiated power $P = \sigma A T^4$. For spheres, $A = 4\pi R^2$, so $P \propto R^2 T^4$. The power ratio is then $P_P/P_Q = (R_P/R_Q)^2 (T_P/T_Q)^4$.

Substituting $R_P/R_Q = 4/3$ and $T_P/T_Q = 5/4$:

$P_P/P_Q = (4/3)^2 (5/4)^4 = (16/9)(625/256)$

Simplifying yields $P_P/P_Q = 625/144$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The difference in length between two rods $A$ and $B$ is 60 cm at all temperatures. If $\propto_A=18 \times 10^{-6} /{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $\propto_B=27 \times 10^{-6} /{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, then the length of $\operatorname{rod} A$ and $\operatorname{rod} B$ at $0^{\circ} C$ is respectively
questions.solution:
The constant length difference of 60 cm at all temperatures implies the thermal expansion terms must cancel. At $T = 0^\circ\text{C}$, $L_{A0} - L_{B0} = 60$.

For arbitrary temperature $T$, the difference is $L_{A0}(1 + \alpha_A T) - L_{B0}(1 + \alpha_B T) = 60$. Substituting the known constant difference yields $(L_{A0}\alpha_A - L_{B0}\alpha_B)T = 0$ for all $T$, requiring $L_{A0}\alpha_A = L_{B0}\alpha_B$.

Given $\alpha_A = 18 \times 10^{-6}/^\circ\text{C}$ and $\alpha_B = 27 \times 10^{-6}/^\circ\text{C}$, we obtain $L_{A0}/L_{B0} = \alpha_B/\alpha_A = 3/2$.

Substituting $L_{A0} = (3/2)L_{B0}$ into the length difference equation gives $(1/2)L_{B0} = 60$, hence $L_{B0} = 120$ cm and $L_{A0} = 180$ cm.

The solution corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The volume of a metal sphere increases by $0.33 \%$ when its temperature is raised by $50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The coefficient of linear expansion of the metal is
questions.solution:
The volume expansion follows $\Delta V = V_0 \gamma \Delta T$, where $\gamma$ is the coefficient of volumetric expansion. With a $0.33\%$ volume increase, we have $\frac{\Delta V}{V_0} = 0.0033$.

The temperature change is $\Delta T = 50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, so $0.0033 = \gamma \times 50$, yielding $\gamma = 6.6 \times 10^{-5} \ /{ }^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

For isotropic materials, $\gamma = 3\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the linear expansion coefficient. Solving gives $\alpha = \frac{6.6 \times 10^{-5}}{3} = 2.2 \times 10^{-5} \ /{ }^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

This corresponds to option A: $\boxed{\text{A}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A black body emits radiation of maximum intensity at wavelength ' $\lambda$ ' at temperature T K. Its corresponding wavelength at temperature $1 \cdot 5 \mathrm{~T} \mathrm{~K}$ will be
questions.solution:
Wien's displacement law states that the product of peak emission wavelength and absolute temperature remains constant: $\lambda_m T = b$, where $b$ is Wien's constant.

Given initial conditions $\lambda_1 = \lambda$ and $T_1 = T$, and final temperature $T_2 = 1.5T$, applying the constant product relation:

$\lambda_1 T_1 = \lambda_2 T_2$

$\lambda \cdot T = \lambda_2 \cdot 1.5T$

Solving for the final wavelength:

$\lambda_2 = \frac{\lambda T}{1.5T} = \frac{\lambda}{1.5} = \frac{2\lambda}{3}$

The peak wavelength at temperature $1.5T$ is therefore $\frac{2\lambda}{3}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A rectangular black body of temperature $127^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ has surface area $4 \mathrm{~cm} \times 2 \mathrm{~cm}$ and rate of radiation is E . If its temperature is increased by $400^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and surface area is reduced to half of the initial value then the rate of radiation is
questions.solution:
Radiation rate from a black body follows Stefan-Boltzmann Law: $P = \sigma A T^4$.

Initial temperature is $T_1 = 127^\circ\mathrm{C} = 400\mathrm{K}$ with surface area $A_1 = 8\mathrm{cm}^2$ and radiation rate $E = \sigma A_1 T_1^4$.

Final conditions: $T_2 = 127^\circ\mathrm{C} + 400^\circ\mathrm{C} = 527^\circ\mathrm{C} = 800\mathrm{K}$, and $A_2 = \frac{1}{2}A_1 = 4\mathrm{cm}^2$, giving $E' = \sigma A_2 T_2^4$.

The ratio is $\frac{E'}{E} = \frac{A_2}{A_1} \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^4 = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{800}{400}\right)^4 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2^4 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 16 = 8$.

New rate is $\boxed{8E}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A body cools from $80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in 5 min . In the next time of ' $t$ ' min, the body continues to cool from $50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The total time taken by the body to cool from $80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is
[The temperature of the surroundings is $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.]
questions.solution:
The temperature of the surroundings is $T_s = 20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Newton's Law of Cooling in approximate finite difference form states:

$\frac{T_1 - T_2}{\Delta t} = K \left( \frac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_s \right)$

First, determine the cooling constant $K$ using the cooling from $80^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in $5\,\mathrm{min}$:

$\frac{80 - 50}{5} = K \left( \frac{80 + 50}{2} - 20 \right) \Rightarrow 6 = K (45) \Rightarrow K = \frac{2}{15}\,\mathrm{min}^{-1}$

Now, apply this $K$ to find the time $t$ to cool from $50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$:

$\frac{50 - 30}{t} = \frac{2}{15} \left( \frac{50 + 30}{2} - 20 \right) \Rightarrow \frac{20}{t} = \frac{2}{15} (20) \Rightarrow t = 7.5\,\mathrm{min}$

The total time to cool from $80^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is $5 + 7.5 = 12.5\,\mathrm{min}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A stationary object at $4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and weighing 3.5 kg falls from a height of 2000 m on snow mountain at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. If the temperature of the object just before hitting the snow is $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and the object comes to rest immediately then the quantity of ice that melts is
(Acceleration due to gravity $=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$, Latent heat of ice $\left.=3.5 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{kg}\right)$
questions.solution:
The object's gravitational potential energy at height $h$ is converted entirely into heat upon impact. Using $g = 10\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-2}}$, the energy released is $mgh = (3.5)(10)(2000) = 70,000\mathrm{J}$.

This heat melts a mass $m$ of ice at $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$, satisfying $mL_f = 70,000$, where $L_f = 3.5 \times 10^5\mathrm{J\cdot kg^{-1}}$. Solving gives $m = \frac{70,000}{3.5 \times 10^5} = \frac{2}{10} = 0.2\mathrm{kg}$.

The mass melted is $0.2 \times 1000 = 200\mathrm{g}$.

The quantity of ice melted is $200\mathrm{g}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two spherical black bodies have radii ' $R_1$ ' and ' $R_2$ '. Their surface temperatures are $T_1 K$ and $T_2 K$ respectively. If they radiate the same power, the ratio $\frac{\mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{R}_2}$ is
questions.solution:
The power radiated by a spherical black body follows the Stefan-Boltzmann law: $P = \sigma A T^4$, where $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $A$ is the surface area, and $T$ is the absolute temperature.

For a sphere, $A = 4\pi R^2$, so $P = 4\pi\sigma R^2 T^4$.

Given two spheres with different radii and temperatures radiating equal power, set the expressions equal:
$4\pi\sigma R_1^2 T_1^4 = 4\pi\sigma R_2^2 T_2^4$

Canceling the common factor $4\pi\sigma$ yields $R_1^2 T_1^4 = R_2^2 T_2^4$.

Solving for the ratio $R_1/R_2$:
$\left(\frac{R_1}{R_2}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^4$
$\frac{R_1}{R_2} = \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^2$

The final answer is $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thermometer bulb has volume $10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^3$ and cross-section of the stem is $0.002 \mathrm{~cm}^2$. The bulb is filled with mercury at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. If the thermometer reads temperature as $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, then the length of mercury column is (coefficient of cubical expansion of mercury $=18 \times 10^{-5} /{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ )
questions.solution:
To determine the height of the mercury column, consider the thermal expansion of mercury when heated from $0^\circ \mathrm{C}$ to $100^\circ \mathrm{C}$. The initial volume is $V_0 = 10^{-6} \mathrm{m}^3$, the cross-sectional area is $A = 2 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{m}^2$, and the cubical expansion coefficient is $\gamma = 18 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{/^{\circ}C}$.

The change in volume is given by $\Delta V = V_0 \gamma \Delta T = (10^{-6}) \times (18 \times 10^{-5}) \times 100 = 18 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{m}^3$.

This volume occupies the stem, so $\Delta V = A L$. Solving for the length: $L = \frac{\Delta V}{A} = \frac{18 \times 10^{-9}}{2 \times 10^{-7}} = 9 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{m} = 9 \mathrm{cm}$.

The correct answer is B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The two ends of a rod of length ' x ' and uniform cross-sectional area ' A ' are kept at temperatures ' $T_1$ ' and ' $T_2$ ' respectively ( $T_1\gt T_2$ ). If the rate of heat transfer is ' $Q / t$ ', through the rod in steady state, then the coefficient of thermal conductivity ' K ' is
questions.solution:
The rate of heat conduction through a rod in steady state follows Fourier's law: $\frac{Q}{t} = KA\frac{T_1 - T_2}{x}$.

Coefficient of thermal conductivity $K$ is obtained by rearranging: $K = \frac{xQ}{tA(T_1 - T_2)}$.

This matches the expression in option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Black bodies $A$ and $B$ radiate maximum energy with wavelength difference $4 \mu \mathrm{~m}$. The absolute temperature of body $A$ is 3 times that of B. The wavelength at which body B radiates maximum energy is
questions.solution:
According to Wien’s displacement law, $\lambda_m T = b$ for any black body, where $\lambda_m$ is the peak wavelength, $T$ is absolute temperature, and $b$ is Wien’s constant.

Given $T_A = 3T_B$, from $\lambda_{mA} T_A = \lambda_{mB} T_B$, substitution yields $3\lambda_{mA} = \lambda_{mB}$.

With $\lambda_{mB} - \lambda_{mA} = 4\,\mu\mathrm{m}$, substitute to obtain $3\lambda_{mA} - \lambda_{mA} = 4\,\mu\mathrm{m}$, so $2\lambda_{mA} = 4\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ and $\lambda_{mA} = 2\,\mu\mathrm{m}$.

Then $\lambda_{mB} = 3 \times 2\,\mu\mathrm{m} = 6\,\mu\mathrm{m}$.

Thus, body B radiates maximum energy at $6\,\mu\mathrm{m}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two bodies A and B at temperatures ' $\mathrm{T}_1{ }^{\prime} \mathrm{K}$ and ' $\mathrm{T}_2{ }^{\prime} \mathrm{K}$ respectively have the same dimensions. Their emissivities are in the ratio $16: 1$. At $\mathrm{T}_1=\mathrm{x} \mathrm{T}_2$, they radiate the same amount of heat per unit area per unit time. The value of $x$ is
questions.solution:
Stefan–Boltzmann Law: The rate of heat radiated per unit area per unit time is given by $P/A = e \sigma T^4$, where $e$ is the emissivity, $\sigma$ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant, and $T$ is the absolute temperature.

Given equal surface areas and equal radiated heat per unit area per unit time, with emissivities in the ratio $16:1$, let $e_A = 16e$ and $e_B = e$.

From $P/A = e \sigma T^4$, equating the expressions for bodies A and B yields $16e \sigma T_1^4 = e \sigma T_2^4$.

Canceling $e \sigma$ (nonzero) gives $16 T_1^4 = T_2^4$.

Substituting $T_1 = x T_2$ results in $16 x^4 T_2^4 = T_2^4$.

Dividing both sides by $T_2^4$ (nonzero) yields $16 x^4 = 1$, so $x^4 = 1/16$ and $x = (1/16)^{1/4} = 1/2$.

The value of $x$ is $0.5$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The temperature of a body on Kelvin scale is ' x ' K . When it is measured by a Fahrenheit thermometer, it is found to be ' x ' ${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$. The value of ' x ' is (nearly)
questions.solution:
Find the temperature where Kelvin and Fahrenheit scales give the same numerical reading.

Let $x$ represent the common numerical value on both temperature scales. The conversion from Kelvin to Celsius is $T_C = T_K - 273.15$. Substituting $T_K = x$ gives:

$T_C = x - 273.15$

The Fahrenheit to Celsius conversion is $T_C = \frac{5}{9}(T_F - 32)$. With $T_F = x$:

$T_C = \frac{5}{9}(x - 32)$

Equating both Celsius expressions:

$x - 273.15 = \frac{5}{9}(x - 32)$

Multiplying through by 9 eliminates the denominator:

$9(x - 273.15) = 5(x - 32)$

Expanding both sides:

$9x - 2458.35 = 5x - 160$

Rearranging terms:

$4x = 2298.35$

$x = 574.5875$

The numerical value where Kelvin and Fahrenheit readings are equal is approximately 574.59.
Among the options, 574 is the closest match.

The correct choice is C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If 120 J of thermal energy is incident on area $3 \mathrm{~m}^2$, the amount of heat transmitted is 12 J, coefficient of absorption is $0.6$, then the amount of heat reflected is
questions.solution:
The total incident thermal energy $Q_{\text{incident}} = 120\text{ J}$ follows the conservation principle: $Q_{\text{incident}} = Q_{\text{absorbed}} + Q_{\text{reflected}} + Q_{\text{transmitted}}$ Given the absorption coefficient $a = 0.6$ and transmitted energy $Q_{\text{transmitted}} = 12\text{ J}$, the absorbed energy is: $Q_{\text{absorbed}} = a \times Q_{\text{incident}} = 0.6 \times 120 = 72\text{ J}$ Substituting into the conservation equation: $120 = 72 + Q_{\text{reflected}} + 12Q_{\text{reflected}} = 120 - (72 + 12) = 36\text{ J}$

Final answer: $\boxed{36\text{ J}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Hot water cools from $80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in 1 minutes. In cooling from $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ it will take (room temperature $=30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ )
questions.solution:
The rate of heat loss by a body is proportional to the temperature difference between the body and its surroundings, as described by Newton's Law of Cooling. The approximate form for finite temperature changes is expressed as:

$\frac{T_1 - T_2}{t} = K \left( \frac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_s \right)$

where $T_s = 30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is the room temperature.

Using the initial cooling data from $80^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in 60 seconds:

$\frac{80 - 60}{60} = K \left( \frac{80 + 60}{2} - 30 \right) \Rightarrow \frac{1}{3} = K (40)$

Solving gives the constant $K = \frac{1}{120} \ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

To find the time $t$ for cooling from $60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $50^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$:

$\frac{60 - 50}{t} = \frac{1}{120} \left( \frac{60 + 50}{2} - 30 \right) \Rightarrow \frac{10}{t} = \frac{1}{120} (25)$

Solving yields $t = \frac{10 \times 120}{25} = 48$ seconds.

The time required is 48 seconds, corresponding to option A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If a black body at 400 K surrounded by atmosphere at 300 K has rate of cooling ' $\mathrm{R}_0$ ', the same body at 900 K , surrounded by same atmosphere, will have rate of cooling nearly
questions.solution:
The rate of cooling for a black body due to radiation follows Stefan-Boltzmann's Law: $R = \epsilon \sigma A (T^4 - T_s^4)$, where $\epsilon = 1$ for a black body.

At initial temperature $T_1 = 400$ K with surroundings at $T_s = 300$ K, the cooling rate is $R_0 = \epsilon \sigma A (400^4 - 300^4) = \epsilon \sigma A \times 10^8 (256 - 81) = \epsilon \sigma A \times 10^8 \cdot 175$.

At temperature $T_2 = 900$ K with the same $T_s = 300$ K, the cooling rate becomes $R = \epsilon \sigma A (900^4 - 300^4) = \epsilon \sigma A \times 10^8 (6561 - 81) = \epsilon \sigma A \times 10^8 \cdot 6480$.

The ratio yields $\frac{R}{R_0} = \frac{6480}{175} = \frac{1296}{35} \approx 37.03$.

Among the given options, this value is closest to 36, indicating the rate of cooling will be nearly $36 R_0$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A rectangular block of surface area A emits energy E per second at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. If length and breadth is reduced to half of initial value and temperature is raised to $327^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ then energy emitted per second becomes
questions.solution:
The Stefan-Boltzmann Law $E = \epsilon \sigma A T^4$ relates the energy radiated per second to surface area and temperature. Given the initial conditions $A_1 = A$ and $T_1 = 300\, \mathrm{K}$, the energy emitted is $E_1 = E$.

When the length and breadth are halved, the surface area becomes $A_2 = A/4$. The temperature is $T_2 = 600\, \mathrm{K}$. The ratio of energies is

$\frac{E_2}{E_1} = \frac{A_2}{A_1} \left( \frac{T_2}{T_1} \right)^4 = \frac{1}{4} \times 2^4 = 4$.

The energy emitted per second becomes $4E$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A centigrade and Fahrenheit thermometer are dipped in boiling water. The water temperature is lowered until the Fahrenheit temperature observed is $140^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$. At that time the temperature registered by the centigrade thermometer is
questions.solution:
Temperature conversion from Fahrenheit to Celsius uses the formula: $T_C = \frac{5}{9}(T_F - 32)$.

For $T_F = 140^\circ\mathrm{F}$, substitute into the formula:

$T_C = \frac{5}{9}(140 - 32) = \frac{5}{9} \times 108 = 5 \times 12 = 60^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

The result corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The following graph represents the radiant power versus wavelength of the black body. The area under the curve represents
options: the maximum wavelength emitted by the object.
the minimum wavelength emitted by the object.
the total energy emitted per unit time by the black body at some particular wavelength
the total energy emitted per unit time per unit area by the black body at all wavelengths.
questions.solution:
The area under the spectral emissive power curve $E_\lambda$ versus wavelength $\lambda$ corresponds to the total energy radiated per unit time per unit area across all wavelengths. This integral $\int_0^\infty E_\lambda d\lambda$ represents the total emissive power, consistent with the Stefan-Boltzmann law $E = \sigma T^4$.

Option A refers to the peak wavelength $\lambda_m$, not the area. Option B is incorrect as minimum wavelength lacks physical significance in this context. Option C misinterprets the integral as a single-wavelength quantity rather than a cumulative measure.

Only option D correctly identifies the area as the total energy emitted per unit time per unit area over all wavelengths.

The correct answer is $\boxed{D}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal sphere cools at a rate of $1.5^{\circ} \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{min}$ when its temperature is $80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. When the temperature of the sphere is $40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, its rate of cooling is $0.3^{\circ} \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{min}$. The temperature of the surrounding $\left(\theta_0\right)$ is
questions.solution:
According to Newton's Law of Cooling, the rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature difference:
$\frac{d\theta}{dt} = -K(\theta - \theta_0)$

Given two measurements:
At $\theta_1 = 80^\circ$C, cooling rate is $1.5^\circ$C/min
At $\theta_2 = 40^\circ$C, cooling rate is $0.3^\circ$C/min

Dividing the corresponding equations:
$\frac{1.5}{0.3} = \frac{80 - \theta_0}{40 - \theta_0}$

Solving for $\theta_0$:
$5(40 - \theta_0) = 80 - \theta_0$
$200 - 5\theta_0 = 80 - \theta_0$
$120 = 4\theta_0$
$\theta_0 = 30^\circ$C

The surrounding temperature is therefore $30^\circ$C.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body cools from $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in 6 minutes. After next 6 minutes its temperature will be (Temperature of the surroundings is $10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ )
questions.solution:
Newton's Law of Cooling provides the relation $\frac{T_1 - T_2}{t} = k \left( \frac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_s \right)$, where $T_s = 10^\circ \mathrm{C}$ is the ambient temperature.

Using the initial cooling data: from $T_1 = 60^\circ \mathrm{C}$ to $T_2 = 40^\circ \mathrm{C}$ over $t = 6$ minutes, we substitute into the formula:
$\frac{60 - 40}{6} = k \left( \frac{60 + 40}{2} - 10 \right)$
$\frac{20}{6} = k (50 - 10)$
$\frac{10}{3} = 40k$
$k = \frac{1}{12} \text{min}^{-1}$

For the next 6 minutes, cooling continues from $T_1' = 40^\circ \mathrm{C}$ to $T_3$, with $k = \frac{1}{12} \text{min}^{-1}$:
$\frac{40 - T_3}{6} = \frac{1}{12} \left( \frac{40 + T_3}{2} - 10 \right)$
Multiplying both sides by 12: $2(40 - T_3) = \frac{40 + T_3}{2} - 10$
This simplifies to: $80 - 2T_3 = \frac{20 + T_3}{2}$
Multiply through by 2: $160 - 4T_3 = 20 + T_3$
$140 = 5T_3$
$T_3 = 28$

The temperature after the next 6 minutes is $28^\circ \mathrm{C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A composite slab consists of two materials having coefficients of thermal conductivity K and 2 K , thickness x and 4 x respectively. The temperatures of two outer surfaces of a composite slab are $T_2$ and $T_1$ respectively ( $\mathrm{T}_2\gt \mathrm{T}_1$ ). The rate of heat transfer through the slab in a steady state is $\left[\frac{A\left(T_2-T_1\right) K}{x}\right] f$, where $f$ is equal to
questions.solution:
The thermal resistance for a material is given by $R = \frac{L}{KA}$, where $L$ is thickness, $K$ is thermal conductivity, and $A$ is cross-sectional area.

For material 1 with thickness $x$ and conductivity $K$, $R_1 = \frac{x}{KA}$.

For material 2 with thickness $4x$ and conductivity $2K$, $R_2 = \frac{4x}{2KA} = \frac{2x}{KA}$.

The total resistance for materials in series is $R_{total} = R_1 + R_2 = \frac{x}{KA} + \frac{2x}{KA} = \frac{3x}{KA}$.

Heat transfer rate is $\frac{Q}{t} = \frac{\Delta T}{R_{total}} = \frac{T_2 - T_1}{\frac{3x}{KA}} = \frac{A(T_2 - T_1)K}{3x}$.

Comparing with the given form $\left[\frac{A(T_2-T_1) K}{x}\right] f$, we find $f = \frac{1}{3}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{D}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The co-efficient of absorption and the coefficient of reflection of a thin uniform plate are 0.77 and 0.17 respectively. If 250 kcal of heat is incident on the surface of the plate, the quantity of heat transmitted is
questions.solution:
For any surface, the coefficients of absorption $a$, reflection $r$, and transmission $t$ satisfy the conservation relation $a + r + t = 1$.

Given $a = 0.77$ and $r = 0.17$, the transmission coefficient is determined as $t = 1 - 0.77 - 0.17 = 0.06$.

The transmitted heat equals the product of the transmission coefficient and the incident heat: $Q_{\text{transmitted}} = t \cdot Q_{\text{incident}} = 0.06 \times 250\ \text{kcal} = 15\ \text{kcal}$.

Final answer: $\boxed{15\ \text{kcal}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Black sphere of radius R radiates power P at certain temperature T . If the temperature is doubled, the radius gets doubled. Now the power radiated would be
questions.solution:
The power radiated by a black sphere follows the Stefan-Boltzmann Law: $P = \sigma A T^4$ where $A = 4\pi R^2$ is the surface area.

With initial values $P_1 = \sigma(4\pi R^2)T^4$ and new conditions $R_2 = 2R$, $T_2 = 2T$, the new power becomes:

$P_2 = \sigma(4\pi(2R)^2)(2T)^4 = \sigma(4\pi\cdot4R^2)\cdot16T^4 = 64\sigma(4\pi R^2)T^4$

Recognizing $\sigma(4\pi R^2)T^4 = P_1$, we obtain $P_2 = 64P_1$.

The power increases by a factor of 64.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two rods of different materials have lengths ' $\ell_1$ ' and ' $\ell_2$ ' whose coefficient of linear expansions are ' $\alpha_1$ ' and ' $\alpha_2$ ' respectively. If the difference between the two lengths is independent of temperature then
questions.solution:
Let the initial rod lengths at reference temperature $T_0$ be $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$, with linear expansion coefficients $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$. Their expanded lengths at temperature $T$ are $\ell_1' = \ell_1(1 + \alpha_1 \Delta T)$ and $\ell_2' = \ell_2(1 + \alpha_2 \Delta T)$.

The difference $\ell_1' - \ell_2' = (\ell_1 - \ell_2) + (\ell_1 \alpha_1 - \ell_2 \alpha_2) \Delta T$. For this difference to be temperature-independent, the coefficient of $\Delta T$ must vanish, giving $\ell_1 \alpha_1 = \ell_2 \alpha_2$.

This implies $\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2} = \frac{\alpha_2}{\alpha_1}$, which corresponds to option B.

Final answer: $\boxed{B}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: At certain temperature, rod A and $\operatorname{rod} \mathrm{B}$ of different materials have lengths $L_A$ and $L_B$ respectively. Their co-efficients of linear expansion are $\alpha_A$ and $\alpha_B$ respectively. It is observed that the difference between their lengths remain constant at all temperatures. The ratio $L_A / L_B$ is given by
questions.solution:
\(L_B^{\prime}=L_B\left(1+\alpha_B \Delta \theta\right)\) and \(L_A^{\prime}=L_A\left(1+\alpha_B \Delta \theta\right)\). So that
\(L_B^{\prime}-L_A^{\prime}=L_B-L_S+\left(L_B \alpha_B-L_A \alpha_A\right) \Delta \theta\)
So \(\left(L_B^{\prime}-L_A^{\prime}\right)\) will be equal to \(\left(L_B-L_A\right)\) at all temperature if, \(L_B \alpha_B-L_A \alpha_A=0\)
\([\operatorname{as} \Delta \theta \neq 0] \text { or } \frac{L_B}{L_A}=\frac{\alpha_{A}}{\alpha_B}\)
i.e., the difference in the lengths of the two rods will be independent of temperature if the lengths are in the inverse ratio of their coefficients of linear expansion.

Now the temperature of the black body is changed so that it radiates maximum energy around wavelength $\left(\frac{\lambda_0}{2}\right)$. The power radiated by it will now increase by a factor of

questions.q: A bucket full of hot water is kept in a room. If it cools from $75^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $70^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in $\mathrm{t}_1$ minutes, from $70^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $65^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in $\mathrm{t}_2$ minutes and $65^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in $\mathrm{t}_3$ minutes, then
questions.solution:

& \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}_1 \lt \mathrm{t}_2 \lt \mathrm{t}_3

But $A_1=A_2$ as radii are same

$\left(\alpha_{\text {stect }}=1.3 \times 10^{-5} /{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The black discs $x, y$ and $z$ have radii $1 \mathrm{~m}, 2 \mathrm{~m}$ and 3 m respectively. The wavelengths corresponding to maximum intensity are $200 \mathrm{~nm}, 300 \mathrm{~nm}$ and 400 nm respectively. The relation between emissive power $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{x}}, \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{y}}$ and $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{z}}$ is
questions.solution:
$\begin{array}{ll}
\text { Emissive power } E=\sigma A T^4 & \Rightarrow E \propto A T^4 \\
A=\pi R^2 & \Rightarrow A \propto R^2

Answer: $T_1 / T_2=\frac{1}{3}$, Option 1.

$\begin{aligned}

Concept:
Emissivity(e)
$=\frac{(\text { rate of radiation emitted thourgh a unit area of material) }}{\text { (rate of radiation emitted through a unit area of blackbody) }}$
Stefan-Boltzmann law states that the amount of radiation emitted by a black body per unit area $\varepsilon$ is directly proportional to the fourth power of the temperature $\mathrm{T}$.
$\varepsilon=\sigma \mathrm{T}^4$, where $\sigma$ is the Stefan coefficient.
Therefore, $\varepsilon_1=\mathrm{e}_1 \sigma \mathrm{T}_1^4$ and $\varepsilon_2=\mathrm{e}_2 \sigma \mathrm{T}_2^4$.
It is given that emmisive power of the both spheres of equal radius is the same.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The coefficient of linear expansion of brass and steel rods are $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ respectively. Lengths of brass and steel rods are $l_1$ and $l_2$ respectively. If $\left(l_2-l_1\right)$ is maintained same at all temperatures, which one of the following relations is correct?
questions.solution:
The correct option is (D).
Concept: Length of a metalic rod at a given temperature is given by,
$l=l_0(1+\alpha \Delta T)$
where, $l_0$ is the initial length, $\alpha$ the coefficient of linear expansion and $\Delta T$ the temperature change.
At any given temperature the lengths of the brass and steel rods can be written as, $l_b=l_1\left(1+\alpha_1 \Delta T\right)$ and $l_s=l_2\left(1+\alpha_2 \Delta T\right)$ respectively.
Therefore, at difference of length is given by,
$\begin{aligned} & l_b-l_s=l_1\left(1+\alpha_1 \Delta T\right)-l_2\left(1+\alpha_2 \Delta T\right) \\ & \Rightarrow l_b-l_s=\left(l_1-l_2\right)+\left(\alpha_1 l_1-l_2 \alpha_2\right) \Delta T\end{aligned}$
Since, $l_b-l_{\mathrm{s}}=l_1-l_2$ as the difference of length remains constant.
Therefore, $\left(\alpha_1 l_1-l_2 \alpha_2\right)=0$
So, $\alpha_1 l_1=l_2 \alpha_2$ is the answer.
Since, $l_b-l_s=l_1-l_2$ as the difference of length remains constant.

Perfect black body absorption and emission

A perfectly black body absorbs all incident radiation regardless of wavelength, giving it an absorption coefficient $a = 1$.

A perfectly black body is therefore both a perfect absorber and perfect emitter of radiation.

questions.q: With an increase in temperature, surface tension of liquid (except molten copper and cadmium)
questions.solution:
The surface tension of liquid decreases with rise of temperature. The surface tension of liquid is zero at its boiling point and it vanishes at critical temperature. $\quad$ At $\quad$ critical $\quad$ temperature intermolecular forces for liquid and gases becomes equal and liquid can expand without any restriction. For small temperature differences, the variation in surface tension with temperature is linear and is given by relation

T_{t}=T_{0}(1-\alpha t)

where $T_{t}, T_{0}$ are the surface tension at $t^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ respectively and $\alpha$ is the temperature coefficient of surface tension.
